claims.text: Conventional automotive exhaust catalysts disperse platinum-group metals on an alumina support.
Adding nanostructured CeO2 to an alumina support improves catalytic activity relative to unmodified alumina.
Adding nanostructured CeO2 to an alumina support improves catalyst durability relative to unmodified alumina.
The CeO2 modification permits lower PGM loading while maintaining comparable or better catalyst performance.
Nanostructured CeO2 acts as an oxygen-storage component in the catalyst support.
The oxygen-storage function of CeO2 enhances catalyst redox cycling.
CeO2 promotes improved PGM dispersion by reducing PGM sintering.
Ceria's oxygen-buffering capacity accelerates oxidation of harmful exhaust compounds.
Interaction between ceria and the PGM produces smaller PGM particles.
Interaction between ceria and the PGM stabilizes PGM particles against degradation.
The combined oxygen-buffering and PGM-stabilization effects improve catalytic conversion.
The combined oxygen-buffering and PGM-stabilization effects prolong catalyst life.
Under simulated exhaust conditions, the CeO2-doped catalyst is expected to improve conversion efficiency and durability by approximately 10–20%.
The CeO2-doped catalyst is expected to sustain similar or better performance with approximately 20–30% less PGM than the baseline catalyst.
The expected improvements require uniformly dispersed CeO2 and an optimized CeO2 loading.
Non-optimal CeO2 particle size or dispersion may prevent the expected improvements.
Exhaust-gas composition and operating temperature may alter the magnitude of the catalyst improvements.
The proposed control and CeO2-modified catalysts will be prepared with identical PGM amounts.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in conversion efficiency and durability is defined as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome and falsification rule concern maintaining performance at 20–30% lower PGM loading, but the experimental design specifies identical PGM amounts for the control and CeO2-modified catalysts. The proposed two-arm experiment therefore cannot directly test the reduced-PGM claim without an additional reduced-loading CeO2 arm.
